chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Sandy Williams and the Jimmy Harrison swing style
summary: Williams was closest to Harrison's swinging, melody-based style, which Benny Morton also had; Jackson laments playing melody is now a lost art.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let's hold it for a second, Butter, just to get our breath together.
We've got to wind this up, too. Yeah, we're still on these trombone players. Before we forget it, you mentioned Sandy Williams.
Sandy Williams. To me, now, he was the closest to Jimmy Harrison, --
Uh-huh. How was that style -- How would you describe that style?

It was a swinging style. They had a lot of swing to it, a lot of little lip trill things, you know, in spots. But it was like you could take a melody and swing it. And Bennie Morton had that knack of taking the melody and swinging, just take the melody and swing it and add just enough little things in there so that you still would know it
was the melody. Yet and still he would improvise, you see.
But not getting too far away from the melody, which is an art within itself.
Today that's a lost art, I think, of playing the melody.
And Sandy was with Fletcher's band for a while, too, Fletcher Henderson. He really fitted in the band. He was in -- In fact, him and J. C. Higgenbotham was in there together.
Sandy and J. C. were there together?
